headlines.article_text: Stock market movers: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, speaking on CNBC's Squawk Box on Sept. 28th, 2026. CNBC The stock market is kicking off the week on a strong note following a losing week. That wasn't the case for every name, however. Nvidia fell in early trading after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. But despite Nvidia's declines, other semiconductor names held up well in early trading. Follow below as CNBC breaks down the biggest stock market moves of the day: 1 Min Ago Here’s why energy stocks are falling Oil prices surged about 20% on Monday as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran continued, raising fears of prolonged disruptions to energy supplies. Anton Petrus | Moment | Getty Images Energy stocks are falling as oil prices retreat from recent highs. Oil prices fell Monday after President Donald Trump said Sunday that renewed strikes on Iran were "highly unlikely" if negotiations made progress. Improving prospects for Middle East diplomacy could reduce fears of supply disruptions, reducing some of the geopolitical risks priced into crude. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 3% to around $87 per barrel. International benchmark Brent slid 4% to about $94 per barrel. Oil futures price trend Energy stocks have faced broader selling pressure as oil prices retreat. Stocks of Exxon Mobil, Chevron , ConocoPhillips , Occidental Petroleum and EOG Resources fell in intraday trading. Sustained declines in crude prices could potentially reduce future revenue and cash-flow expectations for energy companies. Investors are also watching Constellation Energy , NRG Energy and Occidental Petroleum on Monday, followed by financial results from Venture Global , Petrobras and Ecopetrol on Tuesday. Outlooks from these companies could provide fresh clues around oil and gas prices, supply and overall shareholder returns. — Deena Zaidi 24 Min Ago Cruise liners and airline stocks are moving higher as oil prices fall Cruise liners and airline stocks are seeing gains on Monday after oil prices move lower. Shares of Carnival are up 4%, while Royal Caribbean and Norwegian are both up more than 3%. Meanwhile, American Airlines and United Airlines are both moving more than 6% higher while Delta is up 4.6%. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude is down 3.7% to about $87 per barrel. WTI dropped nearly 13% last week on diplomatic headlines, according to FactSet. — Paulina Likos 2 Hours Ago Molson Coors moves lower on JPMorgan downgrade Coors Light beer in 36-packs of cans are stacked at Costco Wholesale store on March 7, 2025 in San Diego, California. Kevin Carter | Getty Images Shares of Molson Coors Beverage slipped 1% following a downgrade at JPMorgan to underweight from neutral. The Coors and Miller parent, which cut its full-year guidance on Thursday, faces challenging fundamentals, including weakness in the beer category and inflationary cost pressures, said analyst Drew Levine. — Michelle Fox 2 Hours Ago JPMorgan upgrades SAP to overweight from neutral Shares for SAP gained nearly 3% after JPMorgan upgraded the Germany-based application software company to overweight from neutral on Monday. "We upgrade SAP to Overweight (from Neutral) as AI moves from pilot to production, a shift we think favors systems of record such as SAP, " wrote Toby Ogg, a analyst at JP Morgan. The firm added SAP's AI offering is improving and raised its price target to £275 from £175. — Ananya Chetia 2 Hours Ago Amazon and Meta rise after JPMorgan makes them top AI picks Thomas Fuller | Lightrocket | Getty Images Doug Anmuth at JPMorgan likes what he's seeing at Amazon and Meta on the AI front, naming the companies in a Monday client note as picks for the bank's analyst focus list. JPMorgan predicts "continued strong revenue growth for Meta on AI-driven ad improvements." The bank sees big revenues over the longer for Amazon, driven by cloud segment growth. "AMZN now expects AWS revenue growth of 40%+ in 2027 & 2028, & for AWS to reach revenue of $1T in the next 5-10 years, w/improving capex payback," Anmuth wrote. Amazon shares are up 3% in the premarket on Monday and Meta is up 2.5%. – Tobias Burns 2 Hours Ago Eli Lilly rises after positive recommendation on key Alzheimer's drug Eli Lilly shares increased nearly 2% after Canada's Drug Agency welcomed a positive recommendation to reimburse Lilly's treatment for early Alzheimer's called Kisunla for eligible adults on Friday. CNBC Berkshire Hathaway ticked 0.4% lower after reporting third quarter earnings Saturday. Some of the key takeaways from the quarter included operating earnings falling 6% year over year, reflecting declines in insurance business and lower gains on common stock investments. Berkshire Hathaway also stepped up share repurchases in Q3. — Paulina Likos 3 Hours Ago DraftKings slips after UBS downgrade The sport betting stock fell 1.7% after UBS downgraded DraftKings to neutral from buy while cutting its price target to $22 from $48. Analyst Robin Farley cited "uncertain regulatory outlook" in prediction markets making it difficult to value DraftKing's core business alone. Making matters more murky, UBS noted is the company recently lowering its core 2026 revenue guidance while guiding for roughly $1 billion of prediction market losses through 2027. The firm raised its estimates for future revenue and earnings per share. Mike Blake | Reuters Eli Lilly on Monday said its obesity pill Foundayo significantly reduced the severity of obstructive sleep apnea, the most common sleep-related breathing disorder, in patients with obesity, in a late-stage trial. The drugmaker plans to file by the end of the year for U.S. approval of the daily pill for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA, in adults with obesity or who are overweight. The results make the pill — which rolled out in the U.S. in April — one of several GLP-1 treatments to show promise in treating the condition. OSA refers to interrupted breathing during sleep due to narrowed or blocked airways, which can cause drops in oxygen and increases in blood pressure that are associated with serious complications, such as hypertension, heart failure and stroke. The condition affects nearly 1 billion adults globally, including 80 million people ages 20 and over in the U.S., according to the National Council on Aging. Most have never been diagnosed, Lilly said in a release. Lilly's blockbuster weight loss injection Zepbound became the first medication to win U.S. approval for OSA in December 2024. Patients have limited treatment options outside of that drug and many use cumbersome machines that provide positive airway pressure, or PAP, to allow for normal breathing. "Foundayo is already making a difference for people living with obesity, and with plans to submit these results to the FDA by the end of the year, we could have the opportunity to help people living with OSA," Dr. Thomas Seck, senior vice president of product development of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health, said in a release. Lilly's sleep apnea trial results The trial tested Foundayo in two independent studies, the first of which included 363 patients who were unable or unwilling to use PAP therapy. The second study included 349 people who were on PAP therapy for at least three months at the time of screening and continued that treatment during the trial. Patients in both studies who took Foundayo started at a low dose and increased it gradually at four-week intervals to different maximum dosages. Researchers specifically examined how much the pill reduced the so-called apnea-hypopnea index , or AHI, which records the number of times per hour a person's breathing shows a restricted or completely blocked airway. The index is used to evaluate the severity of obstructive sleep apnea and the effectiveness of treatments for the condition. People who took Foundayo and were not using PAP therapy had an average of 21.1 fewer AHI events per hour at 52 weeks, compared with an average reduction of 4.8 per hour for the placebo, according to the results. Foundayo also met the trial's second goal in that group, leading to an overall AHI reduction of 43.8% compared with a decrease of 6.3% for the placebo. Lilly said 31.5% of the participants in the Foundayo group met the criteria for remission or improvement to mild OSA. Meanwhile, patients who were on both Foundayo and PAP therapy had an average of 18.3 fewer AHI events per hour at 52 weeks, compared with an average reduction of 5.5 per hour for the placebo. Foundayo led to an overall AHI reduction of around 27.5% in that group, compared with a decrease of 3% for the placebo. The company said 19.6% of the participants on Foundayo and PAP therapy also met the criteria for remission or mild OSA. Foundayo also reduced what's known as the sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden — a measure of how deeply and for how long oxygen levels fall during sleep. That metric fell by 55.9% in people not using PAP therapy and 45.8% in those using it. Lilly said the pill also helped patients lose roughly 11% of their weight across groups at 52 weeks and helped to lower a marker of inflammation. The company said the safety data and how well patients tolerated Foundayo were generally consistent with previous trials on the pill. headlines.title: Amazon's Astro home robot has fans but looks destined for the 'trash heap.' Why it's trying again
headlines.summary: Amazon has formed a new home robotics team and is hiring for a “new-to-world robot product,” according to CNBC’s analysis of job posts.
headlines.article_text: Amazon is building a new home robot after Astro. Here's what we know Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon has formed a new home robot team and is hiring for a “new-to-world robot product,” according to CNBC’s analysis of job posts. The company has tried to break into the consumer robotics market before with the launch of its $1450 Astro device in 2021, but the product never made it out of beta. Recent advances in artificial intelligence and robotics technology have kickstarted a new wave of humanoid development. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jeff Bezos made a bold bet in 2017. A sci-fi and robotics enthusiast, Bezos was convinced that consumers would have a robot in their home in the not-too-distant future. The Amazon founder and then-CEO told a group of the company's top device executives to get to work on building one, and within a few years, the team came up with the $1,450 Astro . The public got its first look at Astro, essentially an Alexa -equipped tablet on wheels that can autonomously navigate a home, recognize faces and act as a roving security monitor, when it rolled on stage at Amazon's fall 2021 event. But it never evolved beyond an invite-only product. Astro shipped to just a few thousand customers, some of whom now believe the robot's days are numbered. The company also released an Astro for businesses in 2023, before sunsetting it less than a year later. Amazon isn't giving up on Bezos' dream of a household robot just yet, despite its stumbles with Astro. Over the past several months, the company has assembled a new team that's working on a "new-to-world robot product," according to a CNBC analysis of job posts. "Robots are about to step out of the movies and into our homes," a recent job listing for an engineer, which has since been removed, stated. The post details a product capable of navigating "dynamic home environments" and "autonomous operation alongside family members." Amazon is known for making long-term bets at the risk of "being misunderstood" in the short term if it gives the company an early advantage in new markets, like it did with the Alexa voice assistant or Kindle e-reader. CEO Andy Jassy reminded investors of this approach in his latest annual letter , where he said artificial intelligence and robotics were among the "biggest inflections of our lifetime." "We try to anticipate what will make customers' lives easier and better every day, and invent the next inflection," Jassy wrote. Analysts also expect the humanoid market to surge in the coming years. Barclays forecast in a January report that the global market, which it currently values at $2 billion to $3 billion, could reach roughly $40 billion by 2035, or as high as $200 billion "under the most optimistic scenarios." While being operated remotely, Fauna Robotics' new robot named Sprout shows off its dexterity in New York, Jan. 14, 2026. Seth Wenig | AP Earlier this year, Amazon redeployed much of the team behind Astro and brought in an MIT roboticist to work on the home robot project, LinkedIn profiles show. It also made a splashy acquisition to supercharge the effort. In March, Amazon scooped up New York-based Fauna Robotics , which has built a 3.5-foot-tall humanoid called Sprout. At the time, the company said Fauna would become part of a new division dubbed the Personal Robotics Group. Some Personal Robotics Group staffers previously worked in Amazon's Lab126 R&D unit, which has been behind many of Amazon's most successful consumer hardware products, like the Kindle e-reader, Echo smart speakers, Fire TV and Fire Tablet. Lab126 was also behind one of Amazon's biggest flops, the Fire Phone . It's unclear what kind of home robot the group is developing, or the types of tasks it could handle, but a June job posting hinted at an effort to "create robots that are not just functional, but delightful." Amazon could be looking to adapt Fauna's robots for homes or businesses. The Sprout humanoid, which was designed to be "friendly and capable" with expressive yellow eyebrows, has primarily been used by developers, as well as commercial and academic researchers . An Amazon job posting published online in October describes a "Field Support Engineer" who can assist with customer support and on-site repair, while another listing seeks a user experience designer to "define what it feels like to live with a Fauna robot." "Our goal is simple: make robots people actually want to live and interact with in everyday human spaces," the listing states. Amazon spokesperson Brad Glasser told CNBC in a statement that the company acquired Fauna because it's "committed to tackling the challenges that can unlock the personal robotics category." "We're optimistic about a future where personal robots are helping people in meaningful ways in everyday life, and we intend to play an important role in making that future a reality," Glasser said. Glasser noted that there remains a substantial gap between what's possible in a controlled lab and what's possible in settings like the living room or a lobby. Amazon is working with the robotics community to solve these challenges, he said. In this screengrab, Amazon Astro is introduced during Amazon Devices and Services Announcement on Sept. 28, 2021. Jamie McCarthy | Getty Images Emily Lugo Velez has been living with the Astro in her North Carolina home since 2023. Lugo Velez, who worked in IT and now runs an AI advisory business, said she and her husband weren't fazed by the robot's $1,000-plus price tag and quickly joined the waitlist. "We spent so much money on this thing," Lugo Velez, 52, said in an interview. "I feel like we're just stuck with it, and we'll let it run around the house until it eventually dies, then send it to the trash heap." She said she still uses the device to check on her pets and appliances when she's out of the house. But beyond that, Astro has primarily become a party trick and a "trip hazard." Most days, she tells Astro to go back to its charging dock. Executives who worked on Astro had discussed making it more capable by attaching an arm to pick up and inspect items without breaking them, said Ken Washington, who served as Amazon's VP of consumer robotics until 2023. He told CNBC that he pushed for a bipedal robot, but leadership disagreed. "We had Jeff [Bezos] in for show and tells and reviews, and I watched his body language pretty closely," Washington said. "I think he was disappointed with the lack of functionality, but I think he was impressed with its ability to map and navigate an undefined space under all lighting conditions." For all the struggles with Astro, Amazon has a rich history in robotics. The company acquired Kiva Systems for $775 million in 2012, which introduced mobile robots to its vast fulfillment network. Since then, Amazon's warehouse automation efforts have ballooned to over one million robots across its facilities that can pick, sort and ferry items to workers. But homes offer unique obstacles for robots to navigate. "The home is a completely different space," said Jeff Burnstein, president of the trade group Association for Advancing Automation, who has been in the robotics industry for 45 years. "Children, pets, grandparents, stairways.
